title: A breach in the news: what to read, what to do
body_md:
## The headline is not your exposure

The headline lands over breakfast: a service you use has been breached, millions affected. Your stomach drops before you have read a word of the article. A car recall works the same way. “Two million vehicles” tells you nothing until you know whether yours is among them, which part is faulty and what the garage will do about it. A breach notice answers those questions too, if you know where to look.

Start with the organization’s own notice, on its site or in its app, and check what kind of announcement it is: an intrusion, an investigation and a confirmed exposure are three different statements. A news story may count every customer when only some records were touched. In the notice, look for **who is affected**, **which data**, **when it happened and when it was found**, **what is still uncertain** and **what the organization will do about it**. If the notice is vague, write the uncertainty down instead of filling the gap with the worst case. And never type a real password into a “breach checker” you reached from an unexpected email.

### What was taken decides what you do

If a password, or the scrambled form a service stores in its place (a hash), may have been exposed, change it on the affected service and change any identical or similar password elsewhere. Use a unique password for each account and turn on multi-factor authentication (MFA). “Hashed” is not an all-clear. How well a hash holds up depends on the scheme, the salt, the work factor, the strength of the password itself and whether the database was really obtained. NIST’s standard for identity services calls for passwords to be stored salted and run through a deliberately costly hash, so that guessing offline is slow, but a notice seldom says enough for you to judge. Nor does “hashed” mean every password has been cracked. Change the ones that matter, and don’t pretend to know how long a crack would take.

If only names and email addresses were exposed, expect approaches that use those details, and verify future account messages independently. Don’t assume a takeover is under way. If payment or identity data was exposed, use the official channels of the provider and your bank for the steps that fit. Credit freezes and IdentityTheft.gov are US-specific; other countries have different systems. If a card was involved, ask its issuer what to do rather than assuming every card must be replaced. And if you spot a transaction you didn’t make, act quickly and follow the issuer’s dispute process.

### A count of reports is not a rate

The FTC’s Consumer Sentinel Network Data Book for 2024 sums up reports sent to a database that US law enforcement uses. The FTC says these are **unverified reports, not a population survey**, so they can’t tell you the odds that your own account was caught in a particular breach. A breach-monitoring service can show known exposures linked to an address, but not appearing there proves nothing: coverage is partial and updates lag. Weigh the service’s notice and your own account checks together.

### Notice or bait?

A real provider may well email you about a breach. That doesn’t make the email’s links the place to start. Open the provider’s app, or type its address yourself, find the security notice and follow the instructions for your own account. Keep the notice and its date in case you need to talk to support. And don’t pass someone else’s personal details on to a group chat or a public forum.

**A calm sequence:** confirm the notice is real, work out what kind of data it covered, protect the accounts or payments tied to it, watch for the specific risk, and when the concrete jobs are done, stop.

widget_config.goal: Read a breach notice for who is affected, what data was exposed, when it happened and what to do, then match your response to the exposure that actually occurred.
widget_config.today_action: Check one important account for a reused password, replace any reuse with a unique one, and turn on multi-factor authentication (MFA) where it is offered.
widget_config.scope: A general method for reading notices. The examples are invented. The FTC’s identity and credit remedies are specific to the US, and no notice, report count or lookup result proves that your data has been misused.

blocks.title: A breach email that wants your password
blocks.situation: A message says a music service has lost its customers’ passwords and offers `https://account-check.example` as a place to “test” your current password. The service’s own app shows no notice yet.
blocks.analysis: The incident itself may be real. The page is the trap: never type a live password into a form somebody sent you. Open the service through its app or an address you know, look for its notice there, and change the password there if that seems warranted.

blocks.title: A narrow notice, posted by the provider
blocks.situation: A service posts a notice inside its own app: a vendor exposed names and postal areas, but no login details and no card numbers. The investigation is continuing.
blocks.analysis: This looks like a genuine, limited incident. Find out whether your record was included, watch for messages tailored to you, and check back for updates. Nothing in the listed data calls for an automatic password reset or a canceled card, though a password you reuse elsewhere deserves fixing anyway.

blocks.title: Sorting a breach notice
blocks.setup: A service you use has posted a notice in its own app. The scenario is invented and contains no real personal data.

steps.prompt: A headline says “millions breached.” What do you read first?

choices.text: Assume every record and every card number has leaked.
choices.consequence: You could spend the day on the wrong problems and miss the real one.
choices.explanation: Headlines rarely say which data or which customers.

choices.text: The provider’s own description of who was affected and which data was involved.
choices.consequence: The size of the headline stops being the size of your risk.
choices.explanation: A big number doesn’t tell you what happened to your account.

steps.prompt: The notice says email addresses and salted password hashes may have been copied, with few details. What now?

choices.text: Change this password on the real service and anywhere you reused it, and turn on MFA.
choices.consequence: You cut the credential risk without needing to know whether the hashes can be cracked.
choices.explanation: A copied hash database calls for action, but not for announcing that your password is certainly cracked.

choices.consequence: Reused and weak passwords stay exposed.
choices.explanation: How well hashes hold up depends on several things, and salt is only one of them.

steps.prompt: A follow-up says card data was not in the affected system. What fits?

choices.text: Cancel every card, just because this service was breached.
choices.consequence: Nothing in the notice justifies the step.
choices.explanation: A breach in one system doesn’t mean every kind of data was kept there.

choices.text: Watch your statements for odd activity, and don’t treat this notice as a reason to replace your cards.
choices.consequence: Your response stays tied to the data that was actually named.
choices.explanation: The notice reports no card exposure.

steps.prompt: An email from the “security team” asks you to re-enter your old password at a new link. What do you do?

choices.text: Ignore the link; look for messages inside the app you know, or reach verified support.
choices.consequence: You walk around a trap set for exactly this moment.
choices.explanation: A breach hands phishers a believable excuse.

choices.text: Enter the old password to prove you were affected.
choices.consequence: The form now holds your credential.
choices.explanation: A provider has no reason to ask for your old password in an emailed form.

blocks.debrief: Run it again with four columns: who is affected, which data, what is still uncertain, what to do. The right action shifts when the facts about the data shift. The independent route stays the same.

questions.prompt: A report says “passwords were hashed” and nothing more. What can you conclude?

choices.text: Neither that they are safe nor that they are cracked; change a password that was affected or reused.
choices.explanation: The scheme, the salt, the cost and the real exposure are all unknown.

choices.text: That every password is certainly safe.

questions.prompt: A US data book collects unverified consumer reports. What does its count represent?

choices.text: The measured probability that any given person will be scammed.
choices.explanation: A count of reports has no measured population behind it, so it can’t give a probability.

choices.text: Reports received, not a rate across the population.
choices.explanation: Only some people report, and the reports are unchecked, so the count can’t be turned into a rate.

questions.prompt: A search of known breaches finds no match for your address. What follows?

choices.text: No match in that service’s known data; keep up your normal account safeguards.
choices.explanation: Its coverage is incomplete and keeps changing.

choices.text: Your address has never turned up in any breach.
choices.explanation: Missing from one database doesn’t mean missing from all of them.

questions.prompt: A verified notice lists names and postal areas and expressly rules out passwords. Where should your attention go first?

choices.text: Tell everyone you know that their passwords were stolen.
Watch for messages tailored to you and follow the updates; the notice gives no reason for a password reset.
choices.explanation: The response matches the data described, and the open questions stay open.
